**Uplift asks who changes because of treatment, not who has a high outcome probability.** A customer who would buy either way may look attractive to an ordinary response model but generate no incremental benefit from a promotion. [1](https://miguelhernan.org/whatifbook)

The four binary potential-outcome types are: helped by treatment (0,1), succeeds either way (1,1), succeeds neither way (0,0), and harmed by treatment (1,0). We do not observe both outcomes for one person, so these are conceptual types rather than known customer labels.

**Estimate conditional average effects instead.** An S-learner uses one outcome model with treatment as a feature. A T-learner fits separate treated and control models and subtracts their predictions. An X-learner uses outcome models to impute effect targets within each group, learns effect models, and combines them.

Evaluate treatment policies on randomized held-out data when available, accounting for uncertainty, capacity, and treatment cost. Accurate outcome prediction does not guarantee accurate effect ranking because subtracting two estimates can amplify error. The deployment decision should target incremental value under a credible causal design.

**Technical details and references.**

Using binary potential outcomes $(Y(0),Y(1))$, persuadables are (0,1), sure things (1,1), lost causes (0,0), and sleeping dogs (1,0). Both potential outcomes are never observed for the same person in an ordinary experiment, so these are conceptual types, not directly identifiable customer labels. The learnable target is usually conditional average treatment effect. [1](https://miguelhernan.org/whatifbook)

An S-learner fits one outcome model using features and treatment; a T-learner fits separate treated/control models and subtracts predictions. An X-learner imputes individual treatment effects using those models, fits effect models within each group, then combines them using weights often related to propensity. Compare on randomized held-out data using policy value or uplift metrics, with uncertainty and capacity constraints. Strong outcome prediction alone does not imply reliable treatment-effect ranking.
